title: Layer Microdissection of Tricuspid Valve Leaflets for Biaxial Mechanical Characterization and Microstructural Quantification
protocol: Retrieve a TV leaflet from the freezer.
Use razor blades, a surgical pen, forceps, a pipette with deionized (DI) water, and a cutting mat for tissue preparation.
Thaw the TV leaflet using 2-3 drops of room-temperature DI water.
Lay the specimen flat on the cutting mat with the ventricularis layer facing upwards.
Position the specimen so that the radial direction aligns with the Y-direction and the circumferential direction aligns with the X-direction.
Examine the chordae insertion locations of the tissue.
Determine an area ideally ~12 x 12 mm with the least amount of large chordae insertions while avoiding extremely thin areas.
Flip the specimen over so that the atrial surface is facing upwards.
Ensure the circumferential and radial leaflet directions remain aligned with the X- and Y-axes, respectively.
Cut a 12 x 12 mm square specimen from the leaflet tissue avoiding large chordae insertions and thin areas.
Remove trimmed portions of the leaflet tissue with forceps and place them into a waste container.
If unable to avoid chordae insertions, cut tissues along the edge of the square specimen.
Place a small dot in the top right corner of the specimen with a surgical pen to track its orientation.
Allow the ink to dry for approximately 30 seconds.
Flip the specimen so the ventricular surface faces upwards.
Trim chordal attachments on the back of the tissue using a razor blade near their insertion location while stretching the chordae from the leaflet.
Flip the specimen again so the atrial surface (the smooth surface) is facing upwards.
Retrieve a noncontact laser displacement sensor.
Zero the displacement sensor on a flat section of the cutting mat near the trimmed tissue.
Position the laser over the central region of the specimen.
Remove air trapped under the leaflet surface to prevent measurement errors.
Use tweezers to push the bubble to the edge of the tissue or lift one corner of the tissue to release trapped air.
Record the thickness shown on the displacement sensor's display.
Repeat two more measurements in other locations of the specimen.
Compute the average leaflet thickness using the three recorded measurements.
Prepare a DI water bath at 37 °C.
Retrieve forceps, the tissue specimen, mounting hardware, a fine-tipped tool, liquid cyanoacrylate glue, and black-painted glass beads (diameter: 300-500 µm).
Mount the tissue specimen to the testing system.
Ensure the circumferential direction of the tissue aligns with the X-direction.
Identify the central one-third square region of the mounted tissue.
Use the approximate corners of this area for fiducial marker placement.
Place glass beads in an open-faced weighing boat.
Create a small pool of liquid cyanoacrylate glue in a separate weigh boat.
Coat the top of the fine-tipped tool with a small amount of glue.
Dab excess glue on the side of the weigh boat.
Gently press the glue-coated tip onto the tissue to create one corner of the central one-third square array.
Grab a glass bead using forceps and carefully place it on top of the glue dot.
Use the camera of the biaxial testing device for help with bead placement.
Repeat steps for three additional beads until the square array is completed.
Ensure the beads are securely attached, and their respective glue dots are not touching or sticking together.
Dry the glue before lowering the tissue into the water bath.
If the beads are stuck together, wait for the glue to dry.
Use forceps to gently grasp the bead or glue and pull it off the tissue.
Create a force-controlled preconditioning protocol in which the tissue will undergo six repetitions of equibiaxial loading.
Set the peak membrane tension Tpeak to 40 N/m with a preload of 3% × Tpeak10.
Set stretch and recovery times of 30 s each for the equibiaxial loading.
Construct an arbitrary testing directory that will temporarily store data for future calculations.
Set the loading rate to be 4.42 N/m.
Construct a new testing parameter set named Preconditioning0.
Set the X-axis control mode to force with a step function.
Set the Y-axis control mode to force with a step function.
Define the load magnitude as fpeak, which is Tpeak multiplied by L.
Set the preload magnitude to 3% of fpeak for only the first repetition.
Specify both the stretch duration and recovery duration as 30 seconds each.
Repeat the protocol 10 times.
Adjust the peak membrane tension if Ppeak exceeds 200 kPa due to tissue thickness effects.
Execute the preconditioning protocol.
Record the X- and Y-dimensions of the specimen after preconditioning.
Determine the time needed for the specimen to achieve the peak equibiaxial configuration at a constant displacement rate.
Calculate loading times for other configurations, specifically TXX:TYY = 1:0.5 and TXX:TYY = 0.5:1.
Manually jog the linear actuators to match the target forces for a given loading ratio.
Record the leaflet dimensions for all loading ratios.
Prepare a displacement-controlled testing protocol that biaxially displaces the tissue from the post-preconditioned configuration.
Set the configurations to TXX:TYY = 1:1, 1:0.5, and 0.5:1 within the times determined previously.
Ensure each protocol has three loading/unloading cycles for repeatability of the mechanical behavior.
Construct a testing directory that will store the data for future calculations.
Name the directory according to the current specimen.
Construct a new testing parameter set with the name 1:1.
Set the X-axis and Y-axis control modes to displacement.
Define the control functions as ramp.
Define the stretch magnitude to be the configuration recorded previously.
Define the preload magnitude as 3% of fpeak for only the first repetition.
Define both the stretch duration and recovery duration as the time recorded in step 1.6.1.
Define the number of repetitions as 3.
Repeat the above steps for the remaining loading ratios (TXX:TYY = 1:0.5 and TXX:TYY = 0.5:1).
Exclude applying preload magnitude for subsequent cycles after the first repetition.
Ensure the stretch magnitude, stretch duration, and recovery duration match those recorded in step 1.6.2.
Only data from the final (third) cycle will be used for stress and strain analyses.
Execute the displacement-controlled protocols.
Return the tissue to its post-preconditioned dimensions after biaxial testing.
Abort the test if the tissue begins to tear.
Submerge the tissue in DI water and mount it to the biaxial testing system.
Perform pSFDI imaging as described in steps 2.1-2.3.
Unmount the tissue.
Proceed to microdissection of intact tissue according to steps 3.1-3.7 if necessary.
Collect histology following step 3.7 if not intact.
Repeat steps 1.2-1.7 with A/S and F/V layers acquired after microdissection.
Use DI water bath for subsequent characterizations on the same day as needed.
Perform digital image correlation of biaxial testing images to determine time-dependent marker positions.
Compute fiducial marker displacements using equation (1).
Consider fiducial markers as a four-node bilinear finite element to compute deformation gradient F using equation (2).
Center the pSFDI device over the specimen.
Turn on the projector and illuminate the specimen with 490 nm (cyan) light.
Open the camera software and inspect the camera's field of view.
Ensure the specimen is centered in the frame and is completely contained within the field of view.
Adjust the digital light processing projector brightness for an intact leaflet specimen, ensuring full illumination without glares on the tissue surface.
Rotate the polarizer across its complete range of motion to detect possible glares or dirt.
Clean the polarizer lens with a microfiber cloth as necessary.
Move the polarizer to its home position aligned with one of the biaxial testing axes.
Capture and save one grayscale image at 0° polarization angle.
Rotate the polarizer by 5° and capture another grayscale image.
Repeat capturing images until 37 images ranging from 0° to 180° in 5° increments are acquired.
Use MATLAB imread() function to construct arrays containing pixel-wise intensities of 37 acquired images.
Arrange these arrays as an n × m × 37 three-dimensional array.
Define the tissue region of interest (ROI) using the grabit() function.
Fit intensity vs. polarizer angle data for each ROI pixel using a 3-term Fourier series.
Determine bi constants through standard linear least-squares regression.
Determine fiber orientation as the polarizer angle associated with the maximum value of I(θ).
Compute the degree of optical anisotropy (DOA) via the given equation.
Visualize acquired fiber orientation and DOA values using plot() and histogram().
Save processed results for later use.
Unmount the tissue from the biaxial tester.
Measure the thickness of the tissue using a laser displacement sensor.
Place the tissue on a wax board.
Examine the ventricularis side for large chordae insertions and note their positions.
Take a photograph of the tissue for reference.
Spread the tissue flat on the wax board with the atrialis facing up.
Affix the tissue to the board using pins in each corner, angled away from the tissue to pull it taut.
Adjust the pin placement slightly to ensure the tissue is taut and in a square configuration.
Place additional pins along the side of the tissue during dissection if necessary to stretch the tissue further.
Remove glass bead fiducial markers from the tissue.
Place DI water on the surface of the tissue using a pipette to completely cover it in a bubble-like manner.
Replenish the DI water as needed throughout the dissection.
Select a corner of the pinned specimen to begin the dissection, avoiding large chordae insertions and extremely thin areas.
Make an initial cut in the A/S layer by lightly dragging the scalpel over the tissue surface along the mounting holes from mechanical testing.
Ensure the cut is at least 5 mm long and the edges start to pull apart, revealing the F/V layer underneath.
Firmly rub along the cut with thin forceps without a sharp tip and pull the edges of the cut apart.
If necessary, lightly trace over the same cut again with the scalpel until it begins to pull apart.
Carefully avoid cutting too deeply into the tissue past the A/S composite layer.
Make a second cut perpendicular to the first cut, ensuring that the two cuts are connected to form a corner.
Run thin tweezers under any small area of tissue separating the two cuts if necessary.
Carefully use scissors to cut through the tissue where the two cuts are not directly connected.
Peel the tissue from the corner.
Rub along the cuts using thin forceps until tissue begins to separate from F/V layer.
Grasp a small piece of separated tissue with tweezers and gently pull to further separate layers.
Place the tip of thin tweezers past the edge of the tissue when grasping.
Switch to larger tweezers for peeling process to prevent ripping and tearing of A/S composite layer.
If separation issues occur, try a different corner as starting point.
Extend the two cuts made for first corner by placing scalpel tip at bottom of each cut and lightly dragging along surface.
Ensure all extension cuts are at least 5 mm and connect with original cuts.
Monitor closely to prevent fibrosa sections from separating with A/S composite layer.
Continue to extend the cuts and peel the top composite A/S layer back while rubbing the seam until one side is finished.
Ensure that the seam between the A/S and F/V composite layers is straight.
Create a second corner perpendicular to the end of the fully peeled side.
Completely separate the A/S layer.
Extend the remaining cuts while avoiding large chordae insertions.
Separate the A/S and F/V layers using rubbing and pulling techniques.
Exclude the chordae insertions from the A/S separation area only when this exclusion allows for an A/S specimen larger than 3.3 mm.
Stop separating the tissue immediately if it tears or a hole forms.
Place scissors in any hole that forms and cut the tissue away from the center to prevent tweezers from being caught.
Begin separating the tissue along another edge to prevent further tearing if the defect forms along the seam of separation.
Look for interlayer connections that may appear while separating the tissue.
Prevent further separation of the tissue without a high risk of ripping.
Carefully cut thin but strong strands using scissors.
Avoid creating a hole in the A/S layer or cutting downwards into the F/V layer.
Continue this process until the largest sample possible of the A/S layer has been separated.
Mark the orientation of the sample using the surgical pen.
Use the scissors to cut along the seam of separation for the remaining tissue edge.
Ensure this cut is as close to the seam of separation as possible.
Place the separated A/S composite layer flat on the cutting mat.
If necessary, use the scalpel to straighten the edges of the tissue and create a square tissue shape suitable for biaxial mechanical testing.
Place the A/S layer in DI water until it is ready to be tested.
Mark the orientation of the F/V layer that remains on the wax board.
Cut the largest square possible out of the area where the A/S layer was removed.
Place this cut-out in DI water.
Excise two strips of tissue—aligned with the circumferential and radial directions—for use in histology.
Use different protocols for the intact and the composite layers (i.e., A/S and F/V).
Take specimens from the tissue pinned to the wax board for the intact layer.
Use the tissue outside the tine/suture holes for the intact leaflet sample.
Collect histology samples after fully completing A/S and F/V composite layers testing and imaging.
Unmount the specimen from the biaxial testing system and lay it flat on a cutting mat.
Excise circumferential and radial strips using a razor blade.
Place excised strips in tissue cassettes.
Submerge the cassettes in 10% formalin for fixation.
Transfer the cassettes to ethanol after 24-48 hours of fixation.
Store the cassettes indefinitely in ethanol until histology processing and staining.
